title: Nobody Knows If Ramayana Just Leaked — and That Might Be the Point
excerpt: A viral clip of Ranbir Kapoor's Lord Ram, questionable VFX, a content creator's deleted comment, and India's most expensive film turning its own marketing into a plot twist worthy of the epic itself
body:
Here's the scene: a blurry, dramatic clip surfaces on X. A figure in traditional attire — bow drawn, body taut — unleashes a devastating arrow at a monstrous, cloud-like demon. The explosion is grand. The build is unmistakably **Ranbir Kapoor**. The VFX? Unmistakably rough.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=3-wSEehDBVk</youtube>

Within hours, the clip had millions of views, a trending hashtag, and an internet that couldn't agree on a single thing about it.

Welcome to July 2026, where **Ramayana: Part 1 — The Introduction** — already India's most expensive film ever made, with a reported budget between ₹835 crore and ₹2,100 crore — has somehow turned its marketing campaign into a mystery thriller more gripping than most films in theatres right now. For many in the Indian diaspora, the *Ramayana* is more than just a story; it's a foundational cultural text, and the prospect of a high-budget, globally-marketed adaptation stirs both excitement and a touch of apprehension, especially given past cinematic attempts.

The clip, posted by the fan account @ramayanafandom on X on July 1, was captioned with breathless excitement: *"Welcome to the #Ramayana Trailer Month: JULY. Trailer 🎬 Posters 🏹 Interviews 🎙️ Global Recognition for Indian Cinema and a leaked trailer snippet of the TRAILER from cinema con."* The implication was clear — someone had secretly recorded footage from a CinemaCon preview, and this was the world's first real glimpse of Ranbir in full battle mode as Lord Ram.

Except maybe it wasn't.

## The AI Theory



> **"Because discussions and criticism across the internet translate into free marketing."

A calculated leak of inferior work from India's most ambitious film?"**


Almost immediately, a counter-narrative emerged. Multiple users on X identified what they said was the original footage — from a completely different production — that had been manipulated using AI to resemble the *Ramayana* aesthetic. The face isn't clearly visible. The movements look processed. And the production house behind director **Nitesh Tiwari's** epic? Complete radio silence. No confirmation, no denial, no legal threats over a leak of what would be the most closely guarded footage in Indian cinema.

That silence is doing a lot of heavy lifting.

## The Deleted Comment

Then it got weirder. Content creator **Dhruv Parikshit**, who recently attended a creators' day event organised by producer **Namit Malhotra** where he met both Tiwari and the film's stars — Ranbir Kapoor and **Yash** — waded into the VFX debate. In a now-deleted Instagram comment, Parikshit made a startling claim: the subpar VFX in *Ramayana*'s April 2 teaser was *intentional*.

> "I also got a chance to talk to one of their VFX artists. He told me that the creators deliberately uploaded a nerfed version of the Rama glimpse. They had better versions of those scenes, yet they intentionally chose to release the incomplete one. Why? Because discussions and criticism across the internet translate into free marketing."

A calculated leak of inferior work from India's most ambitious film? It's either the most audacious marketing play in Bollywood history or the most reckless. Parikshit deleted the comment within hours, but the internet had already screenshotted it into permanence. His replacement was far more diplomatic, praising the character designs as "gorgeous" and "absolutely wonderful" and describing the film as "a beautiful fantasy world set in India."

> "VFX pe kaam chal raha hai, and kaafi accha kaam ho bhi gaya hai... bhai, character designs!! They're gorgeous! It is going to be a great theatrical experience."

## The Adipurush Ghost

The anxiety isn't irrational. In 2023, **Adipurush** — another big-budget adaptation of the Ramayana — became a national punchline for VFX so bad it looked like a mobile game cutscene. The *Adipurush* debacle cost the industry credibility and audiences trust. So when *Ramayana*'s teaser dropped in April with VFX that drew instant comparisons, the PTSD was real. For a film backed by eight-time Oscar-winning VFX house **DNEG** and scored by **Hans Zimmer** and **AR Rahman**, even whispers of bad visual effects carry an existential charge. Many NRIs, who often introduce their children to Indian culture through such films, felt particularly let down by *Adipurush*'s quality, making the stakes even higher for *Ramayana* to deliver.

## So What's Really Happening?

Three things might be true at once. The clip could be AI-generated fan content — the internet manufactures these daily now, and deepfakes of Bollywood stars are practically a cottage industry. The VFX in the April teaser might genuinely have been work-in-progress, released four months before a Diwali premiere while DNEG was still rendering final shots. And the makers might be shrewd enough to let the chaos play out, knowing that every debate, every screenshot, every outraged tweet is another person who now knows the trailer is coming.

And it is coming. The official trailer is expected to premiere at **San Diego Comic-Con** on July 23 — a first for an Indian film at that global stage — followed by a press tour hitting **Toronto**, **London**, and **Tokyo**. This global rollout is a clear signal of the film's international ambitions, aiming to capture the attention of not just the diaspora but also mainstream audiences worldwide. When the real thing drops, every pixel will be measured against the phantom version the internet has spent weeks arguing about.

The cast alone could fill a marquee: **Ranbir Kapoor** as Lord Ram, **Sai Pallavi** as Sita, **Yash** as Ravana, with **Sunny Deol**, **Lara Dutta**, **Ravi Dubey** as Lakshman, and **Arun Govil** — the original television Ram who defined the role for a generation — all circling this epic. The film releases in India on **October 30, 2026**.

**For NRIs and diaspora audiences**, *Ramayana* represents something unprecedented: an Indian mythological epic at a scale that can genuinely compete with Hollywood tentpoles. Whether you'll be watching in New York, London, or Toronto, this is one to mark your calendar for — assuming the trailer lives up to the chaos that preceded it. The film's success could also pave the way for more Indian productions to gain international recognition, a point of pride for many abroad.

Until then, *Ramayana*'s greatest special effect isn't CGI. It's suspense.
